rubric.name: Decision Tradeoff Transparency
rubric.description: Emails about decisions include the options that were considered and why the chosen path was selected. Stating a decision without alternatives is an edict, not communication.

dimensions.label: Names at least one alternative that was seriously considered

Subject: Architecture Review Request: Caching Layer Invalidation Strategy (feedback by [DATE])

---

Hi team,

We're moving forward with adding a caching layer to [system/service name]. I'm asking for architecture feedback on the **invalidation strategy specifically** — implementation details are not in scope for this round.

**The proposal:** [link to design doc]

**What I need from you:**

Please review the invalidation strategy section and share feedback on:
- Whether the chosen approach is sound given our consistency requirements
- Any edge cases or failure modes you see that the design doesn't address
- Concerns about how it interacts with [relevant upstream/downstream system]

**What's out of scope this round:** Implementation specifics, library choices, and rollout sequencing. I'll open a separate thread for those once the invalidation approach is settled.

**Please reply to this thread by [specific date/time].**

---

**For context on the decision already made:**

The proposal uses [chosen invalidation strategy, e.g., event-driven invalidation] rather than [alternative, e.g., TTL-based expiration]. TTL was rejected because [specific reason — e.g., our data mutation patterns are unpredictable enough that stale reads within a TTL window would cause correctness issues in X and Y flows]. The tradeoff we're accepting with event-driven is [e.g., higher operational complexity and a dependency on the event bus being reliable] — that's a known cost, and the proposal addresses it in the [resilience section / linked doc].

If you have questions about the overall caching approach rather than the invalidation strategy, please start a new thread so we can keep this one focused.

Thanks,
[Your name]

Subject: Architecture Review Request: Caching Layer Invalidation Strategy (feedback by [DATE])

---

Hi team,

We're moving forward with event-driven invalidation (rather than TTL-based expiration) for the new caching layer — the full proposal is in the [design doc]. I'm asking for architecture feedback on the invalidation strategy specifically before we move to implementation.

**What I need from you:**

Please review the invalidation strategy section and share feedback on:
- Whether the chosen approach is sound given our consistency requirements
- Any edge cases or failure modes you see that the design doesn't address
- Concerns about how it interacts with [relevant upstream/downstream system]

**What's out of scope this round:** Implementation specifics, library choices, and rollout sequencing. I'll open a separate thread for those once the invalidation approach is settled.

**Please reply to this thread by [specific date/time].**

---

TTL was the main alternative considered. We rejected it because our data mutation patterns are unpredictable enough that stale reads within a TTL window would cause correctness issues in [X and Y flows] — this is documented in the [consistency requirements section] of the design doc.

The cost we're accepting with event-driven is higher operational complexity and a hard dependency on event bus reliability. The design doc addresses this in the [resilience section] — please read that before weighing in, since it covers the mitigations already scoped in.

If you have questions about the overall caching approach rather than the invalidation strategy, please start a new thread so we can keep this one focused.

Thanks,
[Your name]

Subject: Architecture Review Request: Caching Layer Invalidation Strategy (feedback by [DATE])

---

Hi team,

We're moving forward with event-driven invalidation (rather than TTL-based expiration) for the new caching layer — full details in the [design doc](URL). I'm asking for architecture feedback on the invalidation strategy specifically before we move to implementation.

**What I need from you:**

Please review the [invalidation strategy section](URL) and share feedback on:
- Whether the chosen approach is sound given our [consistency requirements](URL)
- Any edge cases or failure modes you see that the design doesn't address
- Concerns about how it interacts with [relevant upstream/downstream system]

TTL was the main alternative considered. We rejected it because our data mutation patterns are unpredictable enough that stale reads within a TTL window would cause correctness issues in [X and Y flows] — see the [consistency requirements section](URL) for the full analysis.

The cost we're accepting with event-driven is higher operational complexity and a hard dependency on event bus reliability. Please read the [resilience section](URL) before weighing in — it covers the mitigations already scoped in, and we're not looking for feedback on those tradeoffs in this round.

If you have questions about the overall caching approach rather than the invalidation strategy, please start a new thread so we can keep this one focused.

Thanks,
[Your name]

Subject: Architecture Review Request: Caching Layer Invalidation Strategy (feedback by [DATE])

---

Hi team,

We're moving forward with event-driven invalidation (rather than TTL-based expiration) for the new caching layer — full details in the [design doc](URL). I'm asking for architecture feedback on the invalidation strategy specifically before we move to implementation. **Please reply to this thread by [specific date, e.g., Thursday, June 19 at 5pm PT].**

**What I need from you:**

Please review the [invalidation strategy section](URL) and share feedback on:
- Whether the chosen approach is sound given our [consistency requirements](URL)
- Any edge cases or failure modes you see that the design doesn't address
- Concerns about how it interacts with [relevant upstream/downstream system]

**What's out of scope this round:** Implementation specifics, library choices, and rollout sequencing. I'll open a separate thread for those once the invalidation approach is settled.

---

**Why event-driven over TTL:**

TTL was the main alternative considered. We rejected it because our data mutation patterns are unpredictable enough that stale reads within a TTL window would cause correctness issues in [X and Y flows] — see the [consistency requirements section](URL) for the full analysis.

The cost we're accepting with event-driven is higher operational complexity and a hard dependency on event bus reliability. Please read the [resilience section](URL) before weighing in — it covers the mitigations already scoped in, and we're not looking for feedback on those tradeoffs in this round.

If you have questions about the overall caching approach rather than the invalidation strategy, please start a new thread so we can keep this one focused.

Thanks,
[Your name]

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that eliminate the need for follow-up meetings. Every email provides enough context for the reader to understand, decide, and act asynchronously. Values decision transparency and thread hygiene.

rubric.name: Decision Tradeoff Transparency
rubric.description: Emails about decisions include the options that were considered and why the chosen path was selected. Stating a decision without alternatives is an edict, not communication.

dimensions.label: Names at least one alternative that was seriously considered
Explains why each alternative was rejected with specific reasoning, not just 'it didn't fit'
Acknowledges what the chosen option sacrifices compared to alternatives
The decision itself appears in the first two sentences, not after paragraphs of context

negative_examples: Deducting points because only one alternative was named when the rubric dimension says 'at least one alternative that was seriously considered'
Keeping the score at 9 after the decision_not_buried issue is fixed in Round 2, then finding a new reason to justify the same score rather than reflecting the improvement
rubric.clarification: If the decision is in the first sentence, one alternative is named with specific rejection rationale, and the tradeoff of the chosen path is explicitly acknowledged — that's a full score. I don't require exhaustive enumeration of every option ever considered. One well-reasoned alternative with a specific rejection rationale and an acknowledged cost is exactly what I want. Round 2 satisfies all four dimensions and should score higher than Round 1, not the same.

rubric.name: Link, Don't Duplicate
rubric.description: Links to existing documents, PRs, dashboards, or design docs replace inline explanations. If information exists somewhere canonical, the email links to it rather than creating a duplicate that will drift.

dimensions.label: References to existing docs, PRs, or dashboards are hyperlinked, not described in prose
Does not reproduce information that's already available at a linked source
Each link has enough surrounding context that the reader knows why to click it

negative_examples: Penalizing a draft for using '[design doc]' placeholder syntax when the email is clearly a template meant to be filled in — the structural pattern is what matters, not whether the URL is live

Scoring Round 2 lower than Round 1 on this criterion when Round 2 references more specific sections (consistency requirements, resilience) and directs readers to those sources rather than reproducing content inline
Treating 'links_to_sources not fully satisfied' as a meaningful deduction when the only issue is placeholder brackets, not a decision to describe docs in prose instead of linking
rubric.clarification: What I actually care about is whether the email's structure uses links as the primary vehicle for detailed information rather than reproducing that information inline. The violation I want penalized is writing out explanations that already exist in a doc — not using bracket placeholders in a template. A draft that says 'see the [resilience section] for mitigations' is doing exactly what I want: pointing rather than duplicating. The placeholder is a fill-in-later artifact, not a structural failure. Round 2 should score higher than Round 1 on this criterion, not lower.
